[Supreme Court]{.status .status-case} [343 U.S. 579](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-343/pdf/USREPORTS-343-579.pdf){.cite} [Decided June 2, 1952]{.cite} [6 to 3]{.cite}
:::

**Holding.** Held the seizure unlawful. No statute authorized it, and the President's powers as Commander in Chief and chief executive did not extend to taking private property at home to settle a labor dispute; that was lawmaking reserved to Congress.

**Question.** Whether President Truman, to avert a strike during the Korean War, could seize the nation's steel mills without statutory authority.

## Why it matters

Justice Jackson's concurrence supplies the framework courts and executive branch lawyers still use. Presidential power is at its maximum when the President acts with Congress's express or implied authorization, in a "zone of twilight" when Congress has said nothing, and at its "lowest ebb" when the President acts against Congress's will. Much of this wiki can be read through it: an [AUMF](../statutes/aumf-2001.qmd) puts the President in the first category, and the [War Powers Resolution](../statutes/wpr-1973.qmd) and funding limits like the [Case-Church Amendment](../statutes/case-church-1973.qmd) are attempts to push contrary action into the third. The majority noted that the [Selective Service Act](../statutes/selective-service-1948.qmd) and the [Defense Production Act](../statutes/dpa-1950.qmd) let the President take property under conditions the government conceded were not met, and Justice Frankfurter's concurrence traced how Congress had withheld seizure power in 1947.

## Status

Good law. Jackson's concurrence, rather than the majority opinion, is the controlling framework in later cases such as [Dames & Moore](../cases/dames-moore-1981.qmd) and [Zivotofsky v. Kerry](../cases/zivotofsky-2015.qmd).

## Statutes at issue

- [Constitution (war powers)](../statutes/constitution-war-powers.qmd){.subj}. Held that the Commander in Chief and executive powers did not authorize a domestic seizure of private property without Congress.
- [Defense Production Act](../statutes/dpa-1950.qmd){.subj}. Its property-taking provisions in Title II did not support the seizure; the government conceded their conditions were not met, and the concurrences found no implied seizure power in the act.
- [Selective Service Act](../statutes/selective-service-1948.qmd){.subj}. Its authority to seize plants under certain conditions did not support the seizure; the government conceded the conditions were not met.

Studied in [Unit 1: Where the power comes from](../study/units/foundations.qmd).
